messages.subject: lavaan Package: Error Message
messages.subject_clean: lavaan Package: Error Message
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I am trying to estimate a growth model using 3 observations per respondent and time-varying covariates. The syntax for the "lavaan" package in R is shown below.

model <- '
  # Intercept and slope with fixed coefficient
  i =~ 1 * LocalBillings_1 + 1 * LocalBillings_2 + 1 * LocalBillings_3
  s =~ 0 * LocalBillings_1 + 1 * LocalBillings_2 + 2 * LocalBillings_3

  # regressions
  i ~ Size1 + Size2
  s ~ Size1 + Size2

  # time-varying covariates
  LocalBillings_1 ~ L11_1
  LocalBillings_2 ~ L11_2
  LocalBillings_3 ~ L11_3
'

However, I get the error message below.

fit <- growth(model,data=TotalRevenue,estimator="ML",control=list(x.tol=1e-6))
Error in lav_model_estimate(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan ERROR: initial model-implied matrix (Sigma) is not positive definite;
  check your model and/or starting parameters.

Your feedback would be greatly appreciated.

Ziad Elmously

messages.body_plain:
First, is the model plausible for your data? If the model badly misfits your data, estimation can be challenging.
     Second, the message says that Sigma is n.p.d. to start. If you supply starting values for parameters. The most critical parameters are probably the variances for i and s. If you set these at positive values away from 0,like
i~~start(0.5)*i
s~~start(0.5)*s
     That might help the initial Sigma to be positive definite.

messages.subject: predict factor scores for n bootstrap samples of a CFA model
messages.subject_clean: predict factor scores for n bootstrap samples of a CFA model
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan-users,

I performed a hierarchical, categorical CFA in lavaan en got the following suggestion from a reviewer, " If the precision of the factor scores is of key interest,
then one might use bootstrap methods to approximate the multivariate distribution of the model parameters and use each instance of the parameter estimates to estimate the factor scores.", which she derived fromt the article of Estabrook and Neale (2013; A Comparison of Factor Score Estimation Methods in the Presence of Missing Data: Reliability and an Application to Nicotine Dependence).

My first idea was to (1) bootstrap the model, (2) to predict factor scores for each seperate bootstrap model, (3) and to average the factor scores final.

Something linke:

bootsamples <- lavPredict(bootstrapLavaan(fit_model, R = 1000L, type = "ordinary", verbose = TRUE, FUN = "coef"), bootsamples, method = "EBM")

Yet I tried a couple of things but I can't  solve the problem that bootstrapLavaan returns a matrix and not a lavaan object. Thus, I cannot predict the factor scores for the seperate samples.

Is there a way to save the bootstrap samples in seperate lavaan objects or to convert the matrix into seperate lavaan objects?

Thank you for sharing your thoughts!

Jes

messages.body_plain:
If you think that i and s have a negative covariance, try a value closer to 0 like -0.3. If i and s each have variances of 0.5 and their covariance is -0.5, then their correlation is -1, making their correlation matrix n.p.d. That produces the second message.
    I am sorry, I gave you bad advice on the first message.If the sample covariance matrix cannot be inverted, then the same matrix itself is n.p.d. That is not a function of model parameters. You need to examine that covariance matrix yourself--if D is your data set, then
>cov(D)
or
>round(cov(D),3)
to round the estimates to 3 decimal places

You may find that the correlation matrix
>cor(D)
makes it easier to see the problem.
     Sorry for the misdirection.

messages.subject: Re: default sample size used when bootstrapping?
messages.subject_clean: default sample size used when bootstrapping?
messages.body_plain:
Happy to be corrected, thanks Stas!  That Rodgers (1999) article I linked to is almost 20 years old, but there was obviously work going on already that he wasn't aware of.

In that case, Olivier, you should use the boot package instead of bootstrapLavaan() so that you can define a function that takes a subsample of a generic (i.e., same N) bootstrap sample.  That is, the function you provide to the "statistic" argument of boot() should have arguments for the data and the indices (rows) to resample from.  By default boot() is just taking the same N, so if you save a bootstrap sample in your user-defined function, you can take a subset of that and perform your analysis.  For example,

> bFunc <- function(data, indices, subN = nrow(data) - 1) {
>   bootData <- data[indices, ]
>   subData <- bootData[1:subN, ]
>   fit <- lavaan(..., data = subData, ...)
>   ...
> }

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: predict factor scores for n bootstrap samples of a CFA model
messages.subject_clean: predict factor scores for n bootstrap samples of a CFA model
messages.body_plain:
> Is there a way to save the bootstrap samples in seperate lavaan objects or to convert the matrix into seperate lavaan objects?

Instead of using bootstrapLavaan(), you can use the boot package directly.  It requires you to define a function that returns that statistic(s) you want bootstrapped estimates of, ideally in a 1-dimensional numeric vector (so that the boot() output will be a matrix, where each row is from a bootstrap sample and each column is a statistic).  Something like this:

> library(boot)
> bootFS <- function(data, indices) {
>   library(lavaan)
>   fit_model <- lavaan(model.syntax, data = data[indices, ])
>   lavPredict(fit_model)
> }

If you just want the average of each factor score across the bootstrap distribution, you can take the column means of the boot() output.  But you can use something like CI width or as a measure of precision, if that is what you are interested in.
>
> boot.out <- boot(data = yourDataFrame, statistic = bootFS, R = 1000)
> ## the output is a list
> summary(boot.out)
> ## the original factor scores are in "t0"
> boot.out$t0
> ## the distribution is in "t"
> colMeans(boot.out$t)
> ## SD of each factor score across bootstrap samples
> apply(boot.out$t, MARGIN = 2, FUN = sd)
> ## You can get CIs from the boot.ci <http://boot.ci>() function.
> ## "index = 1" means the first factor score, so you can loop through the Nth
> (ci.out <- boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(boot.out, type = c("perc", "bca"), index = 1))
> ci.out$perc[4:5]
> ci.out$bca[4:5]

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Dear lavaan-users

I ran the code below yesterday with 10 bootstrap samples (as test run) and it worked perfectly fine. Yet, I tried it today with 1000 samples and discovered that for items which have small amounts of observations on some categories (I am working with ordinal variables), I get bootstrap samples with empty categories and then lavaan can't predict factor scores. The only solution I came up with so far, is to collapse the small categorie together, to decrease the chance of getting bootstrap samples with empty categories. However, this does not really seem statistically sound to me. Is there any other common solution, to prevent getting empty categories through bootstrapping?

Best wishes,

Jes

messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrence and hi lavaan-users,

I have a question with regard to the interpretation of the boot output which I receive for my hierarchical CFA factor model which I established in lavaan. I have seen that the summary(boot.out) reveals a bootSE, which is so far I can see exactly the same value as revealed by: apply(boot.out$t, MARGIN = 2, FUN = sd).

Yet, what I was wondering about is that the boot.out$t function provides you with a matrix that consist of the amount of boostrap samples performed (rows) times the number of observations/persons in your data set (column).

Example --> two bootsrap resampled factor scores (N = 2; to keep it simple for the description) for the last five persons of my data set (N = 931):

        [,927]     [,928]    [,929]     [,930]     [,931]

[1,]  1.305982  0.3882404 -1.366974 -0.5572600 -0.2370531

[2,] -1.217640 -0.4227893  1.083696 -0.4625352  0.5231286

As I understand bootstrapping with replacement, the bootstrap creates a random sample of the observed 'scores', with exactly the same amount of observations/persons, but a different constellation of persons (e.g. original sample --> p1:2, p2:4, p3:7, bootstrap sample: p1:2, p1:2, p3:7 --> in the bootstrap sample person 2 (p2) was not resampled whereas person 1 (p1) was resampled twice).

However, in the matrix I receive from boot(), I get data for exactly the same amount of persons for each bootstrap sample (N = 931), but I am not provided with the information which persons/observations are resampled, is that correct?

What I thus am struggling about is, that if I calculate the column means (separate means for the resampled observations N = 931 across the amount of bootstrap samples, N = 2 --> colMeans(boot.out$t) à revealing 931 means), what does these means tell you? I think that I have anywhere a huge error in my thinking process, because for me it looks like that calculating column means, based on factor scores which basically could be a resampled result from any person in the sample, is just a random mean. If you would know to whom the resampling based factor scores belong, than you could take averages of the n resampled factor scores that belong to the same person, across all established bootstrap samples. But given that (at least that is what it looks like for me) I do not know which of the resampled factor scores belong to which person in the data set, I do not know which resampled factor scores I would have to average across the N = 2 resamples.

Moreover, I have the same problem with the calculation of the sd.

I would be very thankful if anyone could comment on where I am making a fault in my thinking process!

Thanks everyone!

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm analyzing some data I gathered about sensitive behavior with Randomized Response Technique (RRT). The majority of packages to deal with RRT in R adopts modified logistic regressions to treat the response variable, while I would be more interested in fitting a Structural Equation Model (SEM) to model the effect of several drivers on reported behavior.
I found that some authors found a way to model RRT with SEM on the software Mplus (Hox, J., & Lensvelt-Mulders, G. (2004). Randomized response analysis in Mplus. Structural equation modeling, 11(4), 615-620.).
However, I am a satisfied R user and I love the 'lavaan' and 'blavaan' package for latent variable analysis. Would you suggest me a way to fit a SEM on the RRT response with 'lavaan'?

Yours sincerely,

Jacopo Cerri

messages.subject: Re: predict factor scores for n bootstrap samples of a CFA model
messages.subject_clean: predict factor scores for n bootstrap samples of a CFA model
messages.body_plain:
> Yet, what I was wondering about is that the boot.out$t function provides you with a matrix that consist of the amount of boostrap samples performed (rows) times the number of observations/persons in your data set (column).

Only in your case, because the parameters you are saving are the factor score for each person.  If you were bootstrapping CFI, you would only have 1 column.

> However, in the matrix I receive from boot(), I get data for exactly the same amount of persons for each bootstrap sample (N = 931), but I am not provided with the information which persons/observations are resampled, is that correct?

Yes, that's true.  I hadn't considered that in my previous post.  Your factor score in the first column therefore potentially refers to a different person in each bootstrap sample, so the mean of those factor scores is not meaningful.  To make sure you always get the factor scores for your original data, pass your original data.frame to the lavPredict() function's argument "newdata", and add the original data as an additional argument to your function.

> bootFS <- function(data, indices, originalData) {

>   library(lavaan)
>   fit_model <- lavaan(model.syntax, data = data[indices, ])

>   fs <- lavPredict(fit_model, newdata = originalData)
>   fs[,col.number.of.required.factor]
> }

That way your first column of boot.out$t will always refer to the person in the first row of your data set, even if that person wasn't even part of that bootstrapped sample, because lavPredict() will use the model parameters and that person's data to predict what their factor score would be.

Good catch,

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Multigroup analysis
messages.subject_clean: Multigroup analysis
messages.body_plain:
Sorry in advance for the long question. I want to provide enough details.

I wrote some code a couple of years ago to do multigroup analysis with SEM.

I am going to write a simplified version of my code just to make this easier to talk about:

Model <- '
#Latent variables
M =~ C + D
N =~ E + F
FactorA =~ IndicatorA

#Regressions
FactorA ~ M + N
IndicatorB ~ FactorA
'

##########Multigroup analysis)##########################
# Free parameters
fit <- sem(Model, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, data=Data1, missing="fiml", group="Label")
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)

# Loadings constrained
fit <- sem(Model, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, data=Data1, missing="fiml", group="Label", group.equal=c("loadings"))
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)
mi <-modindices(fit, free.remove=FALSE, na.remove=FALSE)
mi[mi$op =="=~",]

# Loadings constrained and regressions constrained
fit <- sem(Model, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, data=Data1, missing="fiml", group="Label", group.equal=c("loadings", "regressions"))
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)
mi <-modindices(fit, free.remove=FALSE, na.remove=FALSE)
mi[mi$op =="~",]

This used to work fine. I obtained modindices for all of the loadings and for the regression paths. However, now when I try to run this code, I get NA for the modindices for the regression "IndicatorB ~ FactorA".

I tried to get around this by turning IndicatorB into a factor. I modified my model to:

Model <- '
#Latent variables
M =~ C + D
N =~ E + F
FactorA =~ IndicatorA
FactorB =~ IndicatorB

#Regressions
FactorA ~ M + N
FactorB ~ FactorA
'

This appeared to fix the problem. Now I could get modindices for the path "FactorB ~ FactorA".

So my first question is: Why do the modindices not work when I include the indicator variable directly in the model?

The other issue is that when I do this, the loading "FactorB =~ IndicatorB" has a significant modindex which tells me that the loading should be different in the different groups. When there is only one indicator, I do not understand what that means. I would have expected the loading to be 1 either way. While this is true for standardized loadings, it is not true for the unstandardized loadings.

So my second question is: Why would a factor loading differ between groups when there is only one indicator variable?

If I constrain the loadings to be the same between groups, then the regression "FactorB ~ FactorA" has a significant modindex. If I let the loading "FactorB =~ IndicatorB" vary freely, then the modindex on the regression "FactorB ~ FactorA" is not significant.

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: Multigroup analysis
messages.subject_clean: Multigroup analysis
messages.body_plain:
On 07/07/2016 11:53 PM, RMH wrote:
> This used to work fine. I obtained modindices for all of the loadings
> and for the regression paths. However, now when I try to run this code,
> I get NA for the modindices for the regression "IndicatorB ~ FactorA".

What changed is this: modindices() no longer computes modification
indices for equality-constrained parameters. It only shows values for
parameters that were not included in the model (and therefore implicitly
set to zero).

To see the 'modification indices' (which are just univariate score
statistics) for equality constrained parameters, use the (new) function
lavTestScore():

lavTestScore(fit)

where you will have 'univariate score tests': these are the modification
indices you are looking for. You may first want to look at the output of
parTable(fit), to learn about the the meaning of the '.p?.' labels.

See http://lavaan.ugent.be/notes/lavaan_eq_constraints.pdf for the
rationale behind this change.

> I tried to get around this by turning IndicatorB into a factor. I
> modified my model to:
>
> Model <- '
> #Latent variables
> M =~ C + D
> N =~ E + F
> FactorA =~ IndicatorA
> FactorB =~ IndicatorB
>
> #Regressions
> FactorA ~ M + N
> FactorB ~ FactorA
> '

But this is not the same model! You add another factor loading here,
which will now be constrained to be the same over groups! One way to get
the same model is using this syntax:

Model2 <- '

#Latent variables
M =~ C + D
N =~ E + F
FactorA =~ IndicatorA

FactorB =~ c(1,1)*IndicatorB
IndicatorB ~~ c(NA,NA)*IndicatorB

#Regressions
FactorA ~ M + N
FactorB ~ FactorA
'

> This appeared to fix the problem. Now I could get modindices for the
> path "FactorB ~ FactorA".

But that is because you used the free.remove=FALSE option. The
modification index for 'FactorB ~ FactorA' does not take the equality
constraint(s) into account. You really should use the lavTestScore()
here (again). For both Model and Model2, they should be the same.

Try this:

fit <- growth(model,data=TotalRevenue,estimator="ML", do.fit = FALSE)

This will NOT fit the data. But still process the model, data, etc...
and give you back a lavaan object that can be inspected.

Next, try:

fitted(fit)$cov

and you will *see* the initial model-implied covariance matrix (Sigma).
Look for covariances that are larger than the corresponding variances.

Finally, add better starting values to avoid this (make sure the implied
variances are large enough).

messages.subject: Re: multilevel modeling
messages.subject_clean: multilevel modeling
messages.body_plain:
On 06/30/2016 11:11 AM, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
>     I wonder if Lavaan handles multilevel models (mixed-effects,
>     hierarchical, random effect models)? It is implied here

>     <http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/10996/r-package-for-multilevel-structural-equation-modeling>,

> No, not in the general sense.  The post refers to partitioning the
> covariance matrix into a Level-1 and a Level-2 covariance matrices, then
> fitting them both using a "multiple-group" model (where each "group" is
> a hierarchical level).

Just as an example (for the record), I once tried to mimic an example
from Joop Hox 2012 book 'Multilevel Analysis', page 232. Syntax below.

Yves.

  library(lavaan)
# Hox Multilevel Analysis example from 'multilevel factor analysis'
# (first edition, 2002, p. 232)

Data <- read.table("peetcomp.dat")
ov.names <- c("wordlist","cards","matrices","figures","animals","occupats")
names(Data) <- c("family", ov.names)

# descriptives
colMeans(Data[,ov.names])
cluster.size <- as.integer(table(Data$family))
nClusters <- length(cluster.size)
N <- sum(cluster.size)

# between sample statistics
DataB <- with(Data, aggregate(Data[,ov.names],
                         by = list(family), FUN = mean))[,ov.names]

# weighted mean
B.mean <- colSums(DataB * cluster.size/N)
# weighted cov
DataBc <- as.matrix(sweep(DataB, 2, STATS=B.mean))
B.cov <- crossprod(DataBc *  cluster.size, DataBc) /  (nClusters - 1)
# note: Hox divides by nClusters, not nClusters - 1
B.cov1 <- crossprod(DataBc *  cluster.size, DataBc) / nClusters

# within
cluster.idx <- as.integer(as.factor(Data[,"family"]))
DataW <- Data[,ov.names] - DataB[cluster.idx,]

W.mean <- colMeans(DataW)
W.cov <- cov(DataW) * (N - 1) / (N - nClusters)

# s (average sample size)
s <- (N^2 - sum(cluster.size^2)) * 1/(N * (nClusters - 1))

# sqrt(s)
# 2.24687

# B.cov.star
B.cov.star <- (B.cov - W.cov)/s

# intra-class correlations
diag(B.cov.star)/(diag(B.cov.star) + diag(W.cov))

# 'MUML' approach, creating 'phantom' latent variables for each
# observed variable at the between level + scaling

# as an ordinary multiple group analysis
model <- '

     # within model
        numeric =~ c(1,1)*wordlist + c(l2,l2)*cards + c(l3,l3)*matrices
        percept =~ c(1,1)*occupats + c(l5,l5)*figures + c(l6,l6)*animals

        numeric ~~ c(f1,f1)*numeric; percept ~~ c(f2,f2)*percept
        numeric ~~ c(f12,f12)*percept

        wordlist ~~ c(r1,r1)*wordlist; cards ~~ c(r2,r2)*cards
        matrices ~~ c(r3,r3)*matrices; occupats ~~ c(r4,r4)*occupats
        figures ~~ c(r5,r5)*figures; animals ~~ c(r6,r6)*animals

     # between model

        # scaling
        bwordlist =~ c(0,2.24687)*wordlist
        bcards    =~ c(0,2.24687)*cards
        bmatrices =~ c(0,2.24687)*matrices
        boccupats =~ c(0,2.24687)*occupats
        bfigures  =~ c(0,2.24687)*figures
        banimals  =~ c(0,2.24687)*animals

        # between model
        bgeneral =~ c(0,1)*bwordlist + c(0,NA)*bcards + c(0,NA)*bmatrices +
                    c(0,NA)*bfigures + c(0,NA)*banimals + c(0,NA)*boccupats
        bgeneral ~~ c(0,NA)*bgeneral

        # residual variances between
        bwordlist ~~ c(0,NA)*bwordlist; bcards ~~ c(0,NA)*bcards
        bmatrices ~~ c(0,NA)*bmatrices; boccupats ~~ c(0,NA)*boccupats
        bfigures ~~ c(0,NA)*bfigures; banimals ~~ c(0,NA)*banimals
'

# NOTE: input is B.cov (which IS pd), not B.cov.star
fit <- lavaan(model, sample.cov = list(within = W.cov, between = B.cov),
            sample.cov.rescale = FALSE,
            sample.nobs = list(N-nClusters, nClusters), std.lv <http://std.lv> = FALSE)
summary(fit)

# compare with Table 12.6 page 237

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I want to use lavaan survey package to build a model. My exogenous categorical variables contain some binary and categorical variables. My endogenous variables are categorical variables. Following the instruction, after weighted my data, I first fit a SEM with lavaan. Then I use lavaan.survey package. My question is that it seems lavaan can deal with categorical variable with WLSMV estimator; but the lavaan.survey package can't. The output still shows the ML estimator when using the lavaan.survey. So I was wondering, how to handle categorical variables when using lavaan.survey package. Below is my syntax. Any help will be appreciated. Thank you.

#Tell R that some variables are categorical/ordinal
hfda[,c("H_S",
        "A_S",
        "20Times",
        "Now")] <-
  lapply(hfda[,c("H_S",
                 "A_S",
                 "20Times",
                 "Now")], ordered)
model4 <- 'H_S~T+r+i+R
           A_S~T+r+i+R
           20Times~H_S+A_S+Age+S100+Edu+Fri+Whites+Nonwhites
           Now~Ha_S+A_S+Age+S100+Edu+Fri+Whites+Nonwhites
           20Times~~Now
           H_S~~A_S'
fit <- lavaan(model5, data = hfda, auto.var = TRUE, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
              meanstructure = TRUE, int.ov.free = TRUE)
fit
summary(fit)
fit.survey<-lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit = fit, survey.design = whfda)
fit.survey
summary(fit.survey,fit.measures=TRUE,standardize=TRUE,modindices = TRUE)

messages.subject_clean: How to make reproducible code from sample covariance matrix
messages.body_plain:
> How can i get this to work? How would you extract the data to transform it to written code?

You are using dput() to save the entire matrix (including redundant elements above/below the diagonal.  Read the help page for ?getCov to see that it doesn't accept a full matrix but just the upper or lower triangle.  I'm not sure why you are using dput() the way you are (saving it to an object instead of to a file).  I assume you want to save it to a file you can give to students, so they can read it in from a fresh R session?  Look into the readRDS() and saveRDS() functions to save individual objects

> readRDS(reproducible.data$cov, file = "myCovMatrix.rds")
> ## FRESH R SESSION, read objects from files, saving them as objects in current workspace
> reproduced.data <- readRDS("myCovMatrix.rds")

Or to save an entire workspace (with both the mean vector and covariance matrix), look into the save() function.

> myCov <- fit@SampleStats@cov
> myMeans <- fit@SampleStats@mean
> save(list = c("myCov","myMeans"), file = "myMoments.RData")
> ## FRESH R SESSION, load saved workspace with existing objects
> load("myMoments.RData")

> Should i use fit@SampleStats@cov or fit@SampleStats@mean because it has more decimals?

Arbitrary, the print method only shows 3 decimals, which you can change:

> print(fit@SampleStats@cov, nd = 4)

But the saved objects will have the maximum available precision, regardless of what is printed to the screen.

> For my data i used multiple imputation with 10 datasets, but i can only extract one sample covariance matrix. What is the background of this? Will the covariance matrix i extracted from the fitted model produce the same results as if i used all 10 multiply imputed datasets?

I'm not sure, are you using one of the runMI() functions?  Perhaps one of the authors of those functions knows what is returned.  I know if you use FIML that "sampstat" returns the EM means and covariance matrix, but with multiple imputation it could be either the averaged estimates of the saturated model or just the sample statistics using pairwise deletion.

messages.body_plain:
On 07/13/2016 03:38 PM, Rogier Kievit wrote:
> #Fit constrained growth model
> growthmodelcons<-
>    ' i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4
> s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4
> s~~0*s
> '

The 'growth()' function was perhaps my worst idea when creating lavaan.
All it really does is setting a few auto.* flags in the lavaan()
function, and hope for the best. This works mostly ok in simple
settings. But often, these default options sit in the way. I am
seriously thinking of removing/deprecating this function in lavaan 0.6.
Instead, I would add another operator, to define random effects.

Anyway, in this model, we still have a non-zero covariance between 'i'
and 's', despite the zero variance for 's'. When using the growth()
function, the user should fix it to zero manually:

# using growth

model <- '
     i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4
     s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4

     s ~~ 0*s; i ~~ 0*s
'

fit <- growth(model, data = Demo.growth)
head(predict(fit))

Mplus is smarter than the growth() function: it automatically fixes the
covariance between 'i' and 's' to zero (and gives a nice warning about it).

I would advocate using the lavaan() function instead. The syntax/call
would look like this:

# lavaan

model <- '
     i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4
     s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4

     i ~ 1; s ~ 1; s ~~ 0*s
'
fit <- lavaan(model, data = Demo.growth, auto.var = TRUE)
head(predict(fit))

The lavaan() function does not 'automatically' add a free covariance
parameter. In all my teaching materials, I now consistently use the
lavaan() function when models involve latent variables that are not
simply 'constructs' measured by indicators (in the traditional
factor-analytic sense).

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
On 07/14/2016 12:13 PM, CJ wrote:
> The lavaan code I used a year or two ago, for a cfa model using multiple
> imputation worked perfectly fine. I recently updated all my active
> packages including lavaan, and for the same models I now get the message
> in the subject line.

The problem is related to semTools, which was (and still is...)
accessing internal slots of the lavaan object, and these slots changed
(and will continue to change in the future).

My impression was that the latest version of semTools (0.4-12) works
well (again) with the current lavaan version (0.5-20). I tried this
myself, and had no problems. If you are using these versions, and you
still get trouble, please contact the semTools package maintainer, and
provide the output of sessionInfo()

> require for a manuscript. I suspect using a much older version of lavaan
> might help? If so, how do I install previous versions

Go to

https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/lavaan/

and download an older version (look at the dates to find a version that
you are looking for). Save this file in a local directory (say, c:\tmp
if you are using windows, or /tmp otherwise). Then, in R, you can type:

(windows:)

install.packages("c:/tmp/lavaan_0.5-16.tar.gz", repos = NULL)

(mac/linux:)

install.packages("/tmp/lavaan_0.5-16.tar.gz", repos = NULL)

Do the same for semTools (find the version that was released after the
lavaan version), and you should be able to reproduce your old results.

Yves.

In a path analysis, I analyzed the association between four variables A, B, C and D, using lavaan. The path structure assumes the following relationship:

- C is driven by A and B
- D is driven by A, B and C.

I first tried using the non-transformed data with MLR as an estimator (following https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/3VkpePK4S_c/ShZxTtO_WwAJ). As the data is not continuous, how big of an issue would that be? Would a log-transformation of the data improve the analysis? Or is there an alternative approach using lavaan?
Another question is whether the issue is there for both endogenous variables C and D, or for only D.

Best regards,
Mialy

messages.subject: Re: model fit got worse after allowing two exogenous variables correlated???
messages.subject_clean: model fit got worse after allowing two exogenous variables correlated???
messages.body_plain:
If the variables were exogenous in your model, then they were already correlating freely in lavaan. When you added syntax referencing the variables, you may have changed their status from covariates (outside the model) to variables within the model. As covariates, the variables were unlikely to affect fit, because the model is estimated conditional on the covariates. (There *could* still be effects on fit, but it would be complicated.) But once they became variables within the model, then any constraints on paths from those variables to any other variables could hurt fit.

In AMOS, the variables may have been treated like variables within the model from the beginning, so that relaxing a constraint (allowing a free covariance between the two) improved fit, as one would expect.

messages.body_plain:
> Is there a way by which I could do a chi square ONLY involving the theoretical factors and not the measurement factors?

No, this is all one model, and this issue has nothing to do with the conditional.x argument.  I think what you want is a bifactor model, where the items load on their trait factor as well as one of two method factors (one for positively worded items and one for negatively worded items), with the trait factor(s) uncorrelated with the method factors.  You should easily find descriptions on Google, but you can ask more questions on the much larger general SEM forum SEMNET:

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

The 'x' in conditional.x (which is only in dev 0.5-21, not official
0.5-20) are observed exogenous variables only.

If you have fitted your model, you can use

lavNames(fit, "ov.x")

to extract those exogenous covariates.

Yves.

On Wed, Jul 20, 2016 at 6:21 PM, Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:

> If the variables were exogenous in your model, then they were already correlating freely in lavaan. When you added syntax referencing the variables, you may have changed their status from covariates (outside the model) to variables within the model. As covariates, the variables were unlikely to affect fit, because the model is estimated conditional on the covariates. (There *could* still be effects on fit, but it would be complicated.) But once they became variables within the model, then any constraints on paths from those variables to any other variables could hurt fit.
>

messages.subject: lavaan 0.5-21 needs testing
messages.subject_clean: lavaan 0.5-21 needs testing
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,

I have rolled up a 'release candidate' for lavaan 0.5-21. To install
this version, type in R:

install.packages("lavaan", repos="http://www.da.ugent.be", type="source")

and it should be version 0.5-21.996 (or higher). Please give it a try
and report any issues (the three 'open' issues on
https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/issues are NOT fixed in this version,
but will be fixed in a future update).

The plan is to release this version after my holidays (August 16), and
no later than the end of August. So we have a few weeks for testing.

Some user-visible changes:

- robust RMSEA and CFI values are now computed correctly, see:

Brosseau-Liard, P. E., Savalei, V., & Li, L. (2012). An investigation of
the sample performance of two nonnormality corrections for RMSEA.
Multivariate Behavioral Research, 47, 904-930

and

Brosseau-Liard, P. E., & Savalei, V. (2014). Adjusting incremental fit
indices for nonnormality. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 49, 460-470.
doi: 10.1080/00273171.2014.933697

- SRMR is now displayed in the summary(, fit.measures = TRUE) output in
the categorical case

- in the summary() output, a dot (.) is added in front of the names of
endogenous intercepts, covariances and variances; this is mostly for
teaching purposes, to distinguish between for example residual and plain
variances; the '.' prefix was the least obtrusive way I could think of;
feedback about this is welcome

- the inspect/lavInspect() function will now always return a nested list
in the multiple group setting

- the inspect/lavInspect() function with the "free" argument will now
show a header with equality constraints (if any)

- GLS/WLS (and friends) now work when fixed.x = TRUE

- a new argument conditional.x (TRUE/FALSE) can be used with all
estimators (ML, GLS, (D)WLS)

- a two-way interaction between observed variables can now be specified
in the model syntax by using a colon, for example:

y ~ x1 + x2 + x1:x2

and a product term will be created automatically

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
> Does X2 similar to MI from modification indices?

Yes, a modification index (Lagrange multiplier) is an estimate of how much the chi-squared (X^2) would change if a (set of) parameter(s) were freed.

> Why does my output shows a warning message that "  lavaan WARNING: se is not `standard'; not implemented yet; falling back to ordinary score test"?

That happens when you use a robust estimator.  This function doesn't yet give you estimates of how much the robust (scaled) chi-squared would change; just the unadjusted chi-squared.

messages.body_plain:
> Therefore, my question: How do I have to write the syntax to get the first figure?

Define the factor as a second-order construct with a single indicator (list 2) by fixing the residual variance of list 2 to zero and the "loading" to 1, so that all the residual variance is represented by "resistance to proactive interference"

> resistance to proactive interference =~ 1*list2recall
> list2recall ~~ 0*list2recall
> resistance to proactive interference ~~ NA*resistance to proactive interference

FYI, you can't actually have spaces in the variable names.  If they have spaces in your data frame, rename them replacing spaces with periods or underscores.

Instead, it returns values of 0 in all cases. Until this capability is added, does anyone have a way to work-around the problem?

ModelFit <- sem(Model, data=DATA1, meanstructure = T)
ModelRes <- as.data.frame(residuals(ModelFit, "casewise"))

Many thanks for your help!

Janet Morrison

messages.subject_clean: Advice on running complex model that yields a not positive definite warning
messages.body_plain:
The warning is about an aspect of your results. That aspect is still there. It is (probably) an unexpected result. Therefore, you should not ignore it. A correlation between factors that is beyond 1 could be driven by random sampling error, but many people will take it as a sign of an error in the model.
     You should start by addressing the first message, about a difference in the scaling of observed variables in the model. Such a difference can cause factor-based SEM software to misbehave. This could be the reason why your results includes the unexpected results. You should look at the variances of your observed variables, and make the different variances more similar. If variable A has a variance in the hundreds, while variable B has a variance in the single digits, you can bring them into line by, say, dividing variable A by 10 (the square root of 100). I recommend that you divide by constants, rather than just standardizing the data. Dividing by constants will eliminate the problem without inducing statistical complications.

messages.subject: Re: Any work-around for inability to get "casewise" residuals in lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: Any work-around for inability to get "casewise" residuals in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
> Currently, lavaan will not provide casewise residuals from residuals(,"casewise") for an sem that does not have latent variables (see open issue #44). Until this capability is added, does anyone have a way to work-around the problem?

So this is just a path analysis?  Then you can just calculate residuals manually the way you would for regression models (assuming you didn't use R's convenience functions for an lm() object).  A casewise residual for person i is the difference between that person's observed and predicted values.  To calculate predicted values for a multivariate regression, just save the matrix of predictor variables and the matrix of regression coefficients, then calculate the predicted values by matrix multiplication and subtract them from the observed values.  For example, if your model is X -> M -> Y, then the outcomes are M and Y, and the predictors are X and M.

> predictors <- c("X","M")
> outcomes <- c("M","Y")
> X <- as.matrix(DATA1[predictors])
> X <- cbind(intercept = 1,  X)
> Y <- as.matrix(DATA1[outcomes])
> B <- lavInspect(ModelFit, "coef")$beta[outcomes, predictors]
> int <- lavInspect(ModelFit, "coef")$alpha[outcomes, "intercept"]
> B <- t(cbind(intercept = int, B))
> Y.hat <- X %*% B # regression equation
> E <- Y - Y.hat   # casewise residuals

If you want them back in your data.frame...

> DATA1$M.resid <- E[ , "M"]
> DATA1$Y.resid <- E[ , "Y"]

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Dear all,

Apologies for posting in an old thread - my query relates very directly to the posts here.

I am also trying to constrain an indicator's error variance to >0. However using code analogous to that posted above does not seem to be working.

(I have tried constraining only the variance of the indicator with negative variance, as shown below, I have also tried putting the same constraint on all indicators' variances. If the code above implies different constraints should be set for different indicators - e.g.

var2 > 0

var2 < 0.5

var3 > 0

var3 < 1.5

 - then I do not understand why, but would like to learn.)

Perhaps I am being naïve, but I am fairly confident the model is not misspecified. To explain: the factors here are dimensions of adolescent mental wellbeing (conduct problems, emotional symptoms, hyperactivity), and the items here are teacher-rated categorical indicators (0 = 'Does not apply', 1 = 'Applies somewhat', 2 = 'Certainly applies'). messages.body_plain:
In the default parameterization ('delta'), you can not constrain the
residual variances of categorical indicators. You need the 'theta'
parameterization for this.

Look for posts about theta/delta parameterization in the archive to
learn more.

Yves.

In the default parameterization ('delta'), you can not constrain the
residual variances of categorical indicators. You need the 'theta'
parameterization for this.

Look for posts about theta/delta par

You should do this before you run lavaan. In R, you can type:

mydata$ISEImo2 <- mydata$ISEImo / 10

and then use 'ISEImo2' in your model instead of 'ISEImo'

Yves.

> Any insights on what's going on?

> # dataset
> aa <- c(0,1,1,2,2,2,3,3,4)
> bb <- c(0,1,6,2,3,1,4,2,5) # outcome variable
> cc <- aa
> dd <- aa
> dat <- data.frame(aa=aa, bb=bb, cc=cc, dd=dd)
>
> # 1
> model.a <- '
> lat =~ start(1.)*aa + cc
> # regression model
> bb ~ aa + dd
> '

The error message is very uninformative. I just never anticipated a
latent variable ('lat'), measured by two identical indicators ('aa' and
'cc').

In addition, why do you need std.ov = TRUE? Set this to FALSE, and avoid
using identical variables.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
On 07/22/2016 11:12 PM, Steven Hirsch wrote:

You can skip all of this:

> #I am sure there is a better way to do this
> i84 <- data1$i84
> i105 <- data1$i105
> i160 <- data1$i160
> i412 <- data1$i412
> i431 <- data1$i431
> i264 <- data1$i264
> ri429 <- data1$ri429
> i487 <- data1$i487
> i489 <- data1$i489
> i511 <- data1$i511
> i21 <- data1$i21
> ri83 <- data1$ri83
> i202 <- data1$i202
> i379 <- data1$i379
> ri455 <- data1$ri455
> ri34 <- data1$ri34
> i240 <- data1$i240
> ri266 <- data1$ri266
> i548 <- data1$i548
> i35 <- data1$i35
> i540 <- data1$i540
> age <- data1$age
> gender <- data1$rgender

because lavaan will find the variables names in your data.frame (mydata).

> model1 <- '
> #sp = school problems
> sp =~ i84 + i105 + ri160 + i412 + i431
> #sa = substance abuse
> sa =~ i264 + ri429 + i487 + i489 + i511
> #fp = family problems
> fp =~ i21 + ri83 + i202 + i379 + ri455
> #vsn = violation of social norms
> vsn =~ ri34 + i240 + ri266 + i548 + i35 + i540
> #Regressing on
> sp ~ age + gender
> sa ~ age + gender
> fp ~ age + gender
> vsn ~ age + gender
> '
>
> #creating the fit stat
> fit1 <- cfa(model1, data = data1, estimator = "WLSMV", mimic = "Mplus",
> ordered = c("i84", "i105", "ri160", "i412",
>        "i431", "i264", "ri429", "i487", "i489", "i511", "i21", "ri83",
>        "i202", "i379", "ri455", "ri34", "i240", "ri266", "i548", "i35",
> "i540"))
>
> summary(fit1, fit.measures = TRUE)
>
> Verbose tells me the model stops after 19 iterations due to "False
> Convergence (8)". My hunch is it has something to do with nlminb and its
> default settings.
> Is there a way to set nlminb parameters to mimic what Mplus uses?

Not really. But one thing you could try is to run a few 'Nelder Mead'
simplex iterations before we let nlminb kick in:

fit1 <- cfa(model1, data = data1, estimator = "WLSMV", mimic = "Mplus",
ordered = c("i84", "i105", "ri160", "i412",

         "i202", "i379", "ri455", "ri34", "i240", "ri266", "i548",

"i35", "i540"), control=list(init_nelder_mead=TRUE), verbose = TRUE)

which seems to convergence. If the fit measures are not the same, we
would need to inspect if the sample statistics are the same, and if the
same number of parameters are used in both software packages.

Yves.
